chapter_theme: Akananuru 241 to 260, in the மணிமிடைபவளம் section: paalai poems of women left for wealth and of friends who answer them with the man's memory of their bodies, two elopement poems, kurinji night trysts threatened by the mother's watch and the velan's rite, mullai homecomings by chariot, and marutham refusals in which the friend measures the husband's scandal by public shouts at Venni, Kudal and Kallur. Puram history runs through the roads: Karikal, the Pandyan, the Kosar, the Moriyar, Nanda's treasure, Nannan's Paazhi.

241.reading: The woman tells her friend that, whatever kind words the friend says of the man's untiring, quarrel-free love, he who once never left her side was hers only once: he has crossed the hills where bamboo shoots shrivel, the rains have forgotten the land and the falls have run dry, where a lone old stag that ran after the white mirage taking it for rain lies spent in the hot forest, and where a red-faced she-monkey plays with fallen nelli fruit scattered like round play-pebbles.
241.nuance: The single particle மன் in நமர்மன் carries the poem: he was ours, once. The stag fooled by the mirage (பேஎய் வெண்தேர்ப் பெயல்செத்து) is left as scene, since it does nothing a person of the situation does; a reader may still hear in it the woman's own hope, chasing comfort that the friend's words hold out.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள், வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone across the hills and left her

comparisons.tenor: the scattered nelli fruit, round like play-pebbles

242.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend tells the woman that their mother, not knowing that the man who chased parrots with them from the millet field came to her in love, wants to learn the cause of her daughter's sickness, has set out offerings and brought the ignorant velan for the veri rite; before the goat's life is given, he would do well to come and hold her often, so her slack bangles and wasted shoulders regain their old beauty.
242.nuance: The deadline is exact: மறி உயிர் வழங்கா அளவை, before the kid is slain. The diviner is called அறியா வேலன், the one who does not know, so the rite is mocked even as it threatens to expose the secret. Spoken for the man's ears, the poem presses him to marry.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill grove, the millet field and the velan's rite

comparisons.tenor: the vengai pollen, gold-like
the peacock's plumage, like gems
the girl's beauty, like tender leaves

243.reading: The woman tells her friend that the merciless north wind has come and settled, now that the avarai flowers fall, eengai blooms like red coral, pagandrai opens around the town, the new rains have stopped and the paddy hangs in ripe ears; if they could make him know their lonely state, which is past their bearing, it would be well, but now, with streaming eyes, the pain is theirs alone, and such is the fruit of their old deeds.
243.nuance: She ends not with blame but with தொல்வினைப் பயன், the fruit of former deeds, a word the later ethics books make doctrine; here it explains nothing away and comforts no one. The wind is கண்இல், eyeless or pitiless, the only one who has come.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வற்புறுத்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் ஆற்றேன் என்பதுபடச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman alone while the man is away

comparisons.tenor: the red eengai blossom, like bent-holed coral

244.reading: The man, his work done, tells his charioteer that the bard has come as a messenger, moved by her grief, reporting how she asked her friend, her eyes reddening, whether it is sweet for him there in this cool hour when the dark-winged birds leave their old tree and the opening mullai smells like a wedded woman's hair; so he bids the charioteer yoke the horses fast and drive, for the task is finished.
244.nuance: The woman's question is quoted within the bard's report within the man's speech: three voices nested in fourteen lines. Her words வரினும், வாரார் ஆயினும் (whether he comes or not) put the season's sweetness against his absence; the man answers with action, not words.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றிய தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai's opening at evening and the man's return

comparisons.tenor: the birds' dark wings, like glue-stiff hide dipped in ghee
the mullai's scent, like a wedded woman's hair

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the addressee is the charioteer (வலவ, line 13)

245.reading: The man rebukes his heart, which has driven him toward wealth: if it knows well that she has the strength to hold the house, telling herself he went with good intent to bring wealth dearer than life, then let it go alone through the rainless bamboo tracks where bandit chiefs who live by robbing caravans pledge a wild elephant's tusk for toddy and stroke a child's head in the frontier hamlet, past flame-red ilavam flowers humming with bees and white bones that feed the camel's hunger; as for him, he will not come.
245.nuance: The quoted line உயிரினும் சிறந்த ஒண்பொருள் is what he imagines her saying to steady herself, and it is her steadiness that stops him: he cannot leave a woman who would bear it so well. The camel (ஒட்டகம்) eating bones is a rare beast in this poetry and marks the land as truly far.

colophon.thurai: பொருள் கடைக்கூட்டிய நெஞ்சினைக் கழறித் தலைமகன் சொல்லிச் செலவழுங்கியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man weighs and refuses a parting for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the ilavam's bright red flowers, like flaring fire

246.reading: The friend refuses the husband entry: lord of a rich town where the rough-backed male snail mates with its partner in the deep pond, with the aaral fish and the crab about, they say that yesterday you bathed in the wide river by the kaanji grove with the flower-haired woman you desire; the gossip is louder than the shout at Azhundur on the day Karikal, at the gate of Venni, broke the might of the kings and the eleven Velir, their drums left on the field.
246.nuance: Paranar measures a private scandal by the noise of a dynastic victory, the Chola's own town of Azhundur roaring for Venni. The snail's open mating in a pond full of watchers is the friend's way of telling the man that what he did in the river was seen.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகற்கு வாயில் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's affair and the friend's refusal

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about his bathing

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the woman he bathed with, seen by the town

pairs.situation: he sports with the woman he desires
the open river where he bathed with her
the onlookers whose talk becomes the gossip

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses creatures of the marutham pond in a marutham poem, without leaving its land (porul 7.27)

247.reading: The woman tells her friend that the man who left her pearl-strung breast lonely has no grace: set on wealth, he did not think how hard the forest is, where the fiery-mouthed male bear with its clan, tired of white iruppai blossom, digs at the top of a red anthill, where a killer elephant watches the waste frontier for men, and where flocks of long-necked vultures, hungry for carrion, roost on the high peaks he crossed.
247.nuance: Her charge is அருளிலர், he lacks compassion, not that he lacks love; she reproaches the choice of wealth over care. Every creature on the road is a feeder (bear, elephant, vulture), which makes the land a place that consumes.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு வேறுபட்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man left her for wealth across the waste

248.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend tells the woman a joke: last night, after a hunter spared a boar that had killed his hound and stood guarding its young in a narrow pass because it looked like his own chief holding the path while his army fell back, the hill lord came to the house, his garland torn by the thicket and swinging on his shoulders like the rope on a bull's hump, and their mother saw him, looked straight at my face, said 'you are a fine one!' and went off laughing.
248.nuance: The joke is a warning. The mother has seen the man at the door and chosen, for now, to laugh, as the hunter saw the boar and chose not to shoot; the next sight may not end so lightly, so the man should stop coming by night and ask for her.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகன் கேட்பத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill hunter and the boar, and a night visit

comparisons.tenor: the boar holding the pass, like the hunters' chief
the man's torn garland on his shoulders, like the rope on a bull's hump

iraicchi.act: the hunter sees the boar in the pass, draws his arrow and turns away without shooting
iraicchi.sense: the mother too has seen the lover and let him go with a laugh, a reprieve that will not last if he keeps coming by night

249.reading: The woman asks her friend what the town's long gossip is for, when her young beauty, fine as Vembi, town of Musundai of many spears who daily gives bards gold-horned bulls, garlands, heaps of food, chariots and elephants, is wasting and he shows no grace, having crossed the bamboo hills where Mazhavar in peacock-feather garlands kill a young cow and eat its roast flesh, and the dusty summer wind over that place sounds so like a hungry tiger's roar that the deer herds scatter on every path.
249.nuance: The gossip is idle because there is nothing left to gossip about: the beauty it talks of is already going. Her beauty is measured by a patron's giving, so her worth is set on the scale of puram generosity.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு ஆற்றாளாய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone over the hills and does not return

comparisons.tenor: the woman's young beauty, like Musundai's town Vembi

250.reading: The friend asks the woman what has happened: while they played with their companions on the fragrant dune under the wave-beaten punnai, a man with garland and chaplet left his chariot with his young men, came close praising their sand-house, got no word in reply and went away; since then he has wasted with longing, the fishing hamlet's women talk, and even the shore stays awake at night with us whose bangles slip.
250.nuance: The friend is pleading for the man (குறைநயப்பு): she tells the meeting as a scene the woman herself took part in, and joins the woman's slipping bangles to his wasting, so that the refusal begins to look like a shared hurt.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநோந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai, the dune and the fishing hamlet

occasion.words: தலைமகற்குக் குறைநோந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது

251.reading: The friend tells the woman that the messages have gone, her shoulders will fill out and her pallor fade, for if he hears of their grief he will not stay there even for Nanda's treasure, he who loosened her bangles and went the long way past the rock-cut road the Moriyar's wheels rolled through when they came against Mokur that would not submit, after the Kosar of wind-swift chariots had broken the enemy at the hall of the old banyan, into the teak groves where a tiger that escaped the elephant's tusk lies unguarded.
251.nuance: Mamulanar's long relative clause runs history into the road: the Kosar's victory, Mokur's refusal, the northern Moriyar cutting a road for their chariots. The man's path is laid down by empires, and the friend still bets that the woman's grief outweighs Nanda's gold.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளது வேறுபாடு கண்டு தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend comforts the woman left by the man on the long road

comparisons.tenor: the Kosar's chariots, swift as the wind

252.reading: With the man listening outside, the woman tells her friend that he is not afraid to come alone with one spear down the hill slope where the yali, making the tiger tremble, strikes an elephant's spotted brow and tears out its tusk, but she cannot bear to stay alone with streaming eyes; shall they make some plan, for their strict mother has forgotten sleep like the watchman of a great tank at midnight when the rain has poured and scattered the eengai blossom.
252.nuance: Two kinds of courage face each other: his on the beast-haunted path, hers that fails at home. The mother as a sleepless tank-keeper is a sharp image: she guards the girl as one guards water that may break its banks.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope and its beasts, and a night meeting

comparisons.tenor: the mother, sleepless in her guarding

253.reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep, thinking that pallor spreads each day, her body has changed, the mother frowns and the gossip is louder than the cheering at Kudal when the Pandyan drove out the Kongar, so that she will not live many days: though he has crossed the Ayiri river into the land of Erumai, chief of the Vadugar whose men raid cattle at midnight from the rock-folds, he will think, without wavering, of her shoulders, her breasts, her long hair and her moon-like face with its bright ear-rings.
253.nuance: The friend answers the woman's three fears (her body, her mother, the town) with a catalogue of the body that the man will remember, so the very beauty she thinks is lost becomes the guarantee of his return. The cattle-raid scene is puram matter (vetchi) placed on his road.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிவின்கண் வேறுபட்ட தலைமகட்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is gone across the river, and the friend comforts

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about the woman
the woman's face, like the moon set with a tilakam in the sky
her breasts, like young palm fruit

254.reading: Back from the king's work, the man tells his charioteer that she, who thinks of him whenever she sees the children of the playing troop, praised by grey-haired foster mothers, toddling in golden anklets across the sanded yard, and the red-legged house dove flying short flights with its mate, has had her lonely grief lifted, for at his word the charioteer drove fast through the fragrant forest of thalavam and mullai, the wheels cutting the green crop, and brought them near the town so they might have joy.
254.nuance: What reminds her of him are two pictures of the household: the children and the mated dove. புறவு names the dove in line 5 and the forest in line 16; the poem's homecoming runs from one to the other.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி வந்தெய்திய தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai forest and the return home

comparisons.tenor: the flash of the chariot running through the crop, like a thin streak of lightning

iraicchi.act: the male dove of the house flies short flights together with its mate
iraicchi.sense: the pair that stays together in the house shows the wife what his absence takes from her, and why his return must be quick

255.reading: The woman tells her friend that the man who left for work would come before many days pass, as a great ship splitting the reeking sea, driven night and day by the wind, finds the shore when its pilot sees the bright flame on the tower, if only they had loving people to carry the word that her ornaments slip and her beauty fades, when in their town among cool fields the unjust north wind blows all night into the guarded house, the pagandrai blooms and the paagal hangs from the koothalam leaves.
255.nuance: The ship and the harbour flame are a picture of a sure return, set as a condition (பெறினே, if only we had): the guidance exists for ships, not for her. The wind is அறன்இன்று, without justice, as if it too should keep a law.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் ஆற்றாமை மீதூரத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left for his work

comparisons.tenor: the great ship, like the world risen up
the paagal fruit, rough like a jackfruit's skin

256.reading: The friend refuses the husband: lord of a town where the sharp-clawed tortoise, tired of sleep under the vallai leaves, crawls over the stone, fills its mouth, reels like a palm-toddy drinker, tramples the field and hides under the soft aambal leaf, do not lie, I know your trick; yesterday you enjoyed the new Vaigai flood with a kohl-eyed girl, and though the courtesans' troop hid it, the gossip is louder than the shout in the assembly at Kallur when a man who had taken a girl's beauty and sworn 'I do not know her' was proved false by witnesses, tied to a tree and had ash poured on his head.
256.nuance: The comparison is a threat: the shout she names was raised against a man who denied an affair under oath, and the husband is now denying his. The tortoise, out of its shelter, reeling and then hiding under a leaf, is the husband's night in small.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகற்கு வாயின் மறுத்தது.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's affair and the friend's refusal

comparisons.tenor: the gossip about the husband's day on the Vaigai
the tortoise's reeling gait, like that of palm-toddy drinkers

ullurai.tenor: the husband's night out with the courtesan and his hiding of it

pairs.situation: tired of the home's ease, he goes out
his revelry with the girl in the Vaigai flood
the courtesans' troop hides what he did

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses a creature of the marutham field in a marutham poem (porul 7.27)

257.reading: As they elope, the man tells the woman that, on these summer days when the paathiri blossom wilts, he gathers her full hair, decks it with maraa flowers, and she cannot keep the bees off her honeyed hair, yet she walks well, swinging her bamboo-smooth arms with bangles ringing, on the way through the hills where robbers climb the forked yaa tree to watch the roads, where the fibre an elephant chewed for water serves the salt-merchants as kindling, and where a young bear pulls a white snake out of an anthill.
257.nuance: Praise and danger run together: he admires her walk (வல்லுவை மன்னால் நடையே) in the very lines that list robbers, a thirsty elephant and a bear dragging a snake, so the compliment reassures her and himself.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகாநின்ற தலைமகட்குத் தலைமகன் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers leave together through the waste

258.reading: The man, whose night tryst failed, tells his heart that though it knew she was as hard to reach as the gold the ancient Velir kept in Nannan Uthiyan's guarded Paazhi, it would not accept it; let it perish like a stone falling into a dark cave on the windy hill, for longing for her it came every night by the narrow, snake-haunted path and did not get her, and now, its face dull, it has made itself a laughing-stock to all the world and brought on unending pain.
258.nuance: The colophon's அல்லகுறி is the night signal that turned out false, and the poem is the man's anger at himself, not at her. Paazhi's buried gold is the measure of her guardedness, a puram treasure-story turned into a picture of a girl beyond reach.

colophon.thurai: அல்ல 1குறிப்பட்டுப் பதிப்பெயர்ந்த தலைமகன் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the night journey to a tryst on the hill

comparisons.tenor: the girl, as hard to reach as the gold of Paazhi
the heart, told to perish like a stone falling into a dark cave

259.reading: The friend tells the woman, whose elopement is agreed, that the spears gleam, the young men are ready, garlands and leaf-skirts are made, rain has ended the earth's heat and the trees put out new leaves, the groves look roofed with flowers, the forest is at its best, and the message has come on this evening of milk-white moonlight; so with a steady mind let her take her word: even if the terrace dries and the vayalai and nochchi she tended wither, bearing the grief of the mother who, more innocent than she, loved her so, and facing her brothers' tiger-like pride, let her be strong and hold him to her breast still.
259.nuance: The friend turns the paalai land green for the journey: the season itself has been arranged in the lovers' favour. The withering vayalai and nochchi are the girl's own garden plants, the home she leaves untended. Who bears the mother's grief (அன்னை அல்லல் தாங்கி) is not stated; we read it as the girl, and the closing wish (வலியாய் இன்னும் தோய்க, நின் முலையே) is terse, so the sense is uncertain.

colophon.thurai: உடன்போக்கு நேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend urges the girl to leave with the man

comparisons.tenor: the groves, as if roofed with flowers
the moonlight, spreading like milk
the brothers' pride, like a tiger's

260.reading: With the man listening outside, prompted by her friend, the woman says that as the sun dims, the hills glow, the bees dive into flowers, herons cry on the kandal shore, the crab slips into its hole, the waves fall quiet, the boats stop work, the sky reddens, the paired anril settles in the palmyra's inner frond, the backwater flowers close and the punnai blossom loses its gold, and the day drains away, she wonders what will become of her, she who still longs for the loveless man's mind, at midnight when the old owl hoots and ghosts walk.
260.nuance: Ten clauses of closing (each thing withdraws to its place) end in the one who has no place to go. Spoken for the man's ears, the paired anril in its nest is the reproach the woman will not make aloud.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழியாற் சொல்லெடுக்கப்பட்டுத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore at sunset

iraicchi.act: the paired anril birds settle together in the palmyra's inner frond at nightfall
iraicchi.sense: even the birds are with their mates at dark, while the man leaves her waiting alone through the night

links.note: Both name former deeds as the cause of suffering: the woman's தொல்வினைப் பயன், the Naladiyar's fixed mark that cannot shrink or grow.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar draws from fixed former deeds the lesson that grief is useless, but the Akananuru woman names the same cause through streaming eyes and says she cannot bear it, so the explanation was available to akam speakers long before it was offered as a cure.

links.note: Both weigh wealth against the wife: in 265 she says he held wealth weightier than her; in 245 he imagines her saying wealth is dearer than life and refuses to go.
links.teaches: The same scale of wealth against the wife is read from both ends, and in 245 it is the wife's readiness to accept the man's reason that makes him unable to act on it, a turn the complaint of 265 cannot show.

links.note: Karikal's victory at Venni: Purananuru 66 praises the defeated king who starved himself facing north in shame at his back wound; 246 measures gossip against the victory shout at Azhundur.
links.teaches: The puram poet honours the loser of Venni above the victor while the akam poet borrows only the victor's roar, which shows how differently one battle served praise of honour and a scale for noise.

links.note: Both use the battle of Venni: 55 as Cheralathan's starving to death after his wound, 246 as Karikal's triumph.
links.teaches: Within one anthology the same battle supplies a mother's grief with the image of a death beyond comfort and a friend's scorn with the image of a deafening cheer, so akam poets picked a side of a public event to suit the speaker's mood.

links.note: Both are the friend refusing the husband after he bathed in the river with his woman, and both end 'the gossip is greater than the shout' (ஆர்ப்பினும் பெரிதே) at a historical event.
links.teaches: The repeated frame shows that measuring marutham gossip by a public shout was a fixed form, and the poets made their point by which shout they chose: a Chola victory in 246, a rival's flight in 226.

links.note: Both name the rock-cut road the Moriyar's chariot wheels made: in the Purananuru the sun's disc standing over that pass is the image of the patron's daily charity; here the pass is the far road the lover crossed.
links.teaches: A northern dynasty's road through the southern hills was common knowledge to both kinds of poem, so the same landmark could stand for a patron's open-handedness and for the distance that keeps a lover away.

links.note: Both are the friend's comfort that he will return although he has passed the Moriyar's rock-cut road; 69 says he will not stay long, 251 that not even Nanda's wealth would keep him.
links.teaches: Put side by side the two comforts show that the Moriyar road had become the stock boundary of the far journey, and that 251 sharpens the assurance by setting against it the greatest wealth the poets knew.

links.note: 265's woman asks whether it is the Nandas' treasure hidden under the Ganges that he values more than her; 251's friend says he would not stay even if he got Nanda's wealth.
links.teaches: The Nandas' treasure is the same weight on the scale in both poems, but the woman fears it outweighs her and the friend swears it does not, so the comfort and the complaint are exact answers to each other.

links.note: Both are the friend's comfort that the man, gone past the Ayiri river, will come back because he will remember the woman's body (her thoyyil marks in 177, her face and look in 253).
links.teaches: Together they show the friend's argument from memory of the body as a set move, and 253 adds what 177 lacks, the woman's own fears of mother and town, which the remembered body is offered to outweigh.

links.note: Both measure gossip by a public shout over a royal victory, 253 at the Pandyan's Kudal after the Kongar were driven out, 246 at the Chola's Azhundur after Venni.
links.teaches: In paalai as in marutham the gossip-and-shout frame fits each speaker's land and dynasty, so the formula traveled across thinais while the king named changed with the poet.

links.note: Both show a lighthouse lamp on a tall tower that calls ships to the shore at night: the idyll as a sight of the port on the guide's road, the poem as the pilot's sign of landfall.
links.teaches: The idyll records the harbour light as a fact of the port; the akam poet turns the same light into the sure sign of a voyage's end and sets it against the woman's lack of any messenger, so a civic fixture became an emblem of return.

links.note: Both refuse the husband and measure the gossip by a public shout; 246 names a battle, 256 names an assembly's punishment of a man who falsely denied an affair.
links.teaches: The later poem bends the frame into a threat: the shout it chooses was raised against a man who swore 'I do not know her', exactly the denial the husband is making, so the comparison judges as well as measures.

links.note: Both are the man speaking to his heart about a night meeting and both name Nannan's fortress Paazhi.
links.teaches: Paazhi stands for a well-guarded prize in both of the man's speeches to his heart, rejoicing in 142 and despairing in 258, which shows that a chieftain's fortress had become the akam measure of a girl's inaccessibility.

links.note: 259's friend tells the girl to bear her mother's grief and go; in 55 the mother of an eloped girl says she cannot sleep and wishes her life had left with her daughter.
links.teaches: The friend names the mother's grief only as a weight the girl must carry away with her, while 55 shows from inside that the grief is a wish to die, so the anthology measures the cost the friend's counsel asks the girl to accept.

links.note: Both list the signs of dusk, with the anril calling or settling in the palmyra's inner frond (பெண்ணை அகமடல்) among them.
links.teaches: Kapilar's idyll uses the dusk catalogue as the moment the man promises marriage, while 260 uses the same signs to open a night of dread, so the formula of nightfall was shared and its turn at the end set its meaning.

links.note: 259 is the friend urging the girl to go now the season is right; 257 is the man on the road praising her walk through a summer waste.
links.teaches: Read in order the two poems show the elopement from its promised green season to the real summer road, and the man's praise of her walk answers the friend's request that she go with a steady mind.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage: the formal union that ends secret love, sought or pressed for in the akam poems
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு கடாயது); the verses here imply it

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place and time of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
the diviner of Murugu, whom the mother calls when she reads the girl's lovesickness as possession
the velan's rite of possession by Murugu, and the ground where it is performed
